# Multi-view projection
Also called: Multi-view voxelization, Orthographic multi-view voxelization, 3-pass voxelization

## Overview
Multi-view projection methods convert 3D geometry into a voxel grid by rasterizing the scene from multiple camera viewpoints, typically aligned with the principal axes, to ensure complete coverage and topological integrity (6-separation) [S1, S2, unofficial]. Unlike single-view projection methods which suffer from geometric distortion or gaps when triangle normals are parallel to the view direction, multi-view approaches combine occupancy data from all orthogonal passes to eliminate cracks and missing data [S2, unofficial]. This family is chosen when topological integrity is critical and the performance cost of multiple draw calls or passes is acceptable [S1].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of rasterizing 3D geometry into a 3D voxel space using multiple orthographic projections. The shared mathematical and procedural principles are:

1.  **Coordinate Mapping:** A transformation matrix $M_{voxel}$ maps world-space coordinates to voxel indices. This matrix typically scales by the grid resolution $(V_x, V_y, V_z)$ and translates by the bounding box minimum $B_{min}$ [S1, S2, unofficial].
    $$ M_{voxel} = \text{Scale}(V_x, V_y, V_z) \times \text{Translate}(-B_{min}) $$
2.  **Orthographic Cameras:** Cameras are positioned at a fixed offset beyond the scene bounding box along each principal axis (X, Y, Z) [S1]. The projection frustum is expanded by a scale factor (e.g., $1.02 \times R$) to ensure full coverage [S1].
3.  **Atomic Accumulation:** When rasterizing from multiple views, voxels may be hit by fragments from different passes. To prevent race conditions and ensure correct occupancy, writes to the voxel grid (or intermediate buffers) must use atomic operations [G].
4.  **Degeneracy Handling:** Triangles parallel to the view direction result in degenerate projections (lines). These must be handled by either rasterizing along a different axis or using specific geometric tests to ensure the triangle's volume is captured [S2, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Single 2D Projection Voxelization](3482-single-2d-projection-voxelization.md)
Single 2D Projection Voxelization is a method for producing 6-separating (tunnel-free) voxel grids from planar triangles using only a single 2D rasterization pass along the dominant axis of the triangle's normal vector. It leverages the "thinness" property of voxelization to avoid the redundant projections required by multi-view methods like [Orthographic Multi-View Voxelization](3892-orthographic-multi-view-voxelization.md) or [3-Pass Voxelization](5300-3-pass-voxelization.md). By restricting computation to the axis where the triangle is thickest, it reduces computational cost while maintaining topological correctness through specific edge-crossing tests. See [Single 2D Projection Voxelization](3482-single-2d-projection-voxelization.md) for details.

### [Orthographic Multi-View Voxelization](3892-orthographic-multi-view-voxelization.md)
Orthographic Multi-View Voxelization rasterizes scene geometry into a 3D texture using three orthographic cameras aligned with the scene's bounding box axes to create a voxelized representation for subsequent volume rendering. It differs from [Single 2D Projection Voxelization](3482-single-2d-projection-voxelization.md) by using multiple views to ensure coverage and from [3-Pass Voxelization](5300-3-pass-voxelization.md) by synthesizing the result into a final "worksheet" texture rather than leaving it in intermediate slab buffers. See [Orthographic Multi-View Voxelization](3892-orthographic-multi-view-voxelization.md) for details.

### [3-Pass Voxelization](5300-3-pass-voxelization.md)
3-Pass Voxelization is a rasterization-based technique that eliminates cracks and missing data in voxel grids by rendering the scene from three distinct viewpoints aligned with the principal axes (X, Y, Z). Unlike single-view projection methods which suffer from geometric distortion or gaps when triangle normals are parallel to the view direction, this method ensures complete coverage by combining the occupancy data from all three orthogonal passes. It is chosen when topological integrity (6-separation) is critical and the performance cost of multiple draw calls is acceptable. See [3-Pass Voxelization](5300-3-pass-voxelization.md) for details.

### [Volumetric Representation via Depth Map Registration](6435-volumetric-representation-via-depth-map-registration.md)
This method constructs a 3D volumetric representation from a sparse set of calibrated multi-view images by registering estimated depth maps into a voxel grid. It specifically addresses non-Lambertian scenes by using individual minimum cost per view for depth estimation rather than a global threshold, and represents geometry as a sparse voxel cloud where voxel values indicate the number of views mapping to that location. It distinguishes itself from static voxelization by including an iterative refinement step that cleans scattering voxels and smooths sharp corners to increase coding gain for virtual view synthesis. See [Volumetric Representation via Depth Map Registration](6435-volumetric-representation-via-depth-map-registration.md) for details.

### Multi-View Stereo Cost Volume Construction
**Definition:** A cost volume $V_c$ is constructed from feature volumes $\{Vf_i\}$ of $N$ reference views to perceive coarse scene structure and provide scene priors for sampling, skipping blank areas [S1].
**Parameter:** $L$: Number of depth layers in the cost volume. Typical value: 16 [S1].
**Pitfall:** Checkerboard artifacts caused by deconvolution layers in the Res-Unet processing the cost volume are eliminated by replacing deconvolution with combinations of upsampling and convolution layers [S1].

## Background
The concept of multi-view projection for voxelization originates from the need to create watertight, topologically correct voxel representations for volume rendering and ray marching, where single-view methods often produce artifacts [S1, S2, unofficial]. The 3-pass approach is a standard technique in real-time graphics to ensure 6-connectivity [S1, S2, unofficial]. The use of orthographic cameras aligned with axes simplifies the projection matrix and ensures uniform sampling density across the volume [S1]. The integration of multi-view stereo (MVS) principles, such as cost volume construction, extends these techniques to reconstruct volumes from sparse image sets, particularly for neural rendering applications like NeRF [S1].
